_comment: Criteria reference for the Agentic Compatibility Benchmark — the single source of truth for what each criterion means and why. GOVERNANCE: whenever a criterion changes (tool set, thresholds/anchors, triage filters), update its entry here IN THE SAME CHANGE. Rendered by /criteria (public/criteria.html) and /criteria/<slug> (public/criteria-detail.html). Criteria are displayed with contiguous position numbers (1..N) in array order; the `id` is the internal/data key (kept stable, e.g. Security = 9 in benchmark.json); the `slug` drives the URL. Criteria that were dropped from the benchmark (former C3, C5) are intentionally absent. Path triage filters mirror triage-config.json in this repository.

criteria.name: Clear Domain Boundaries
criteria.one_liner: Modules and services have single responsibilities with no hidden cross-boundary coupling.
criteria.what: Whether the modules a repo declares depend on each other cleanly. Three measurements: circular dependencies and mean fan-out over a tree-sitter code graph, and change coupling — modules that keep being edited in the same commit — read from git history.
criteria.why: Boundaries decide how much of a system has to be understood before one part of it can be changed safely. The code graph is also load-bearing elsewhere: it is the substrate for the critical-path inference Test Coverage is waiting on.

how.tools: graphifyy 0.9.28 (tree-sitter code graph, deterministic and offline; grammars for Elixir, Ruby, Python, TypeScript/JavaScript). External coupling comes from our own call-site detector, not from graphifyy. Change coupling is computed over `git log` across a 90-day window — the metric, its formula and its thresholds are code-maat's, and only the implementation is ours, so pairs can be aggregated at module level directly.
how.anchors: Acyclic Dependencies Principle — 0 circular dependencies between modules. Module fan-out under 5 on average. Change coupling uses code-maat's own command-line defaults (a module needs 5 revisions, a pair 5 co-changes and a 30% coupling degree; commits touching more than 30 modules are swept), so the threshold is a published tool default rather than one we chose.
how.scoring: Mean of the metrics that could be scored. Cycles: 0 green, 1-3 amber, 4+ red. Fan-out: under 5 green, 5-10 amber, over 10 red. Change coupling: 0 undeclared coupled pairs green, 1-5 amber, 6+ red. Gradation inside a band is provisional. A repo where fewer than half its declared modules appear in the dependency graph is reported indeterminate rather than scored. On a stack whose code graph is known to under-resolve, each graph metric is judged separately — graded where the measured value already breaches the green threshold, withheld where it sits inside it. Where nothing is scoreable the criterion is indeterminate, never a default high mark.

nuances.title: Modules are declared, not guessed
nuances.detail: A module is read from the repo's own workspace declaration and its member globs — pnpm-workspace packages (the packages: sequence only, honouring ! negations), an Elixir umbrella's apps_path, npm workspaces, uv workspaces. Walking for manifests would promote Phoenix's assets/package.json to a module. A workspace declaration is authoritative and short-circuits; the sibling-projects layout read is a heuristic and falls through to the lib/, src/, app/ source-namespace fallback when it does not fire.

nuances.title: Layer-organised repos are indeterminate
nuances.detail: A repo organised by architectural layer rather than domain (models, controllers, services) reads indeterminate. Layers legitimately depend on each other, so cycles among them are not defects.

nuances.title: Change coupling is the metric that survives a bad graph
nuances.detail: Two modules that keep being edited in the same commit are behaviourally coupled whether or not anything resolves a symbol between them, which is why this is the one C1 measurement that still works where the extractor under-resolves. A pair counts as a violation only when neither module declares a dependency on the other — the criterion's own hidden cross-boundary dependency. It is withheld, not scored zero, where the ecosystem has no per-module dependency declaration to compare against (there, every pair would be undeclared and the number would mean nothing) and where fewer than two modules reach the minimum revision count in the window (too little history to tell coupling from coincidence). Dependency lockfiles are excluded: one `pnpm up` rewrites every lockfile in a workspace and would couple everything to everything.

nuances.title: Elixir is measured, and graded only where the measurement is a credible floor
nuances.detail: The graph-derived metrics are only as good as the graph. Measured against ground truth rather than assumed: graphifyy resolves an Elixir alias only when the module name is exactly two segments and the file path is its literal lowercase, so Services.Alpha resolves but Services.Alpha.Client and snake_cased names such as Services.TwoWord do not — and real Elixir is overwhelmingly one of those. On one Elixir umbrella it recovered 4 of 8 real cross-app dependencies and reported one of them backwards. The same check on a TypeScript monorepo recovered 5 of 6, so the defect is stack-specific. This is indeterminate rather than pending: we are not committing to repair a third-party extractor.

nuances.title: Withholding is asymmetric: bad news from an under-counting graph is still credible
nuances.detail: Every edge the extractor misses pushes both graph metrics down — a missed dependency lowers fan-out and can erase a cycle outright. A measured value on an under-resolving stack is therefore a floor: the real figure can only be higher. That makes a bad reading trustworthy and a clean reading worthless. A measured 2 cycles means there are at least 2; a measured 0 means nothing. A mean fan-out of 5.5 is already outside the green band whatever was missed; a mean of 2 could be anything. Each metric is judged on its own — graded when the floor already breaches green, withheld when the floor sits inside it. Grading a floor yields the most generous score the evidence supports, which is the right direction to err. Withholding per criterion rather than per metric was tried first, and published a full green on a system whose other metric read amber.

nuances.title: Dependency relations are a denylist with a published audit
nuances.detail: Every extracted graphifyy relation counts as a dependency unless it is explicitly excluded, and the report carries a per-relation count so the classification is inspectable. Excluded, each for a recorded reason: contains, method and defines (structural, file-to-symbol), rationale_for and cites (doc annotations), indirect_call and uses (inferred confidence), and references. references is graphifyy's unresolved bare-name relation: measured across one repo per stack it produced zero cross-module pairs that imports did not already carry, and three demonstrably false ones.

nuances.title: Standard-library and cross-language misresolution are defended against
nuances.detail: graphifyy resolves a module reference by name, so Elixir's require Logger binds to any local logger.ex and Python's import logging binds to any local logging.py. Import-shaped links whose target basename is a standard-library module name for that language are dropped and counted as skipped_stdlib_collision_edges. Links whose two endpoints are in different language families (a .py 'calling' a .ts) are dropped and counted as skipped_cross_language_edges. A cycle direction held up by a single link into a stdlib-colliding filename is surfaced as a finding but excluded from the count.

nuances.title: Degenerate graphs read indeterminate, measured by coverage
nuances.detail: The share of declared modules that appear in the dependency graph is measured and published on every report alongside its threshold of 50%. Below that, the criterion is indeterminate: the extractor did not resolve enough of the repo for a grade to mean anything. The distribution across the benchmark's systems is bimodal — 0% where extraction resolved nothing, 61.5% to 100% everywhere else.

nuances.title: External targets are call-site anchored, and redacted
nuances.detail: A URI literal counts as external coupling only where it sits at a recognised HTTP-client construction, base-URL option, database connection or queue/topic publish. Unanchored literals — asset URLs, seed data, social links, SVG xmlns, JSON-schema ids — are rejected and the rejected count is published. Test, fixture, mock, cassette and __mocks__ paths (the shared path allowlist) are excluded, as are build output, vendored trees and minified bundles. Documentation and placeholder domains and hostnames with no dot never count. Outbound call targets are emitted as host only: connection strings can carry credentials, so userinfo, path and query are stripped before anything is written.

nuances.title: No Vue, Svelte or Astro parser — a known gap for Vue-heavy frontends
nuances.detail: The installed grammar set omits these despite the tool's documentation. Component edges from Vue single-file components, Svelte files and Astro files are absent from the code graph. A repo where no file type produces parseable edges is indeterminate and left unscored. A repo whose other code does parse is scored on an incomplete graph — Vue-side cycles go undetected and mean fan-out reads lower than reality, so a Vue-heavy frontend in a TypeScript workspace appears cleaner than it is.

nuances.title: The graph metrics see only the declared top-level modules
nuances.detail: Cycles and fan-out are measured between the units the repo declares. Tangling inside one workspace member is invisible to them, so a green on those two metrics is a statement about the declared boundaries and not about internal structure. Change coupling is not bounded that way, since it reads what people actually edited together. Boundary-violation trend — the same graph, diffed over time — is still to come.

criteria.name: Documented APIs
criteria.one_liner: Public interfaces carry descriptions an agent can read, not just names and types.
criteria.what: Description coverage of the system's public API surface. GraphQL fields and REST/OpenAPI operations, parameters and response-schema properties are pooled into a single percentage.
criteria.why: Introspection gives an agent names and types. It does not say what a field means, which values are safe to send, or what an endpoint does to the system. An agent that cannot read the contract cannot safely call it.

how.tools: Nothing is compiled. Elixir systems are read from the code itself — Absinthe schemas and phoenix_swagger definitions, parsed as AST by helper scripts. Any other stack is measured from a committed artifact: an OpenAPI document (JSON or YAML) or a GraphQL SDL file. Ruby is declared N/A. test, spec and .agents trees are skipped so support schemas do not pad the denominator.
how.anchors: 0 undescribed public elements. Introspection is not documentation.
how.scoring: Linear: 5 × described ÷ total, pooled across GraphQL and REST so a system carrying both is judged on one number. The criterion is left unscored rather than scored low when it does not apply, when no schema or artifact is found, and when REST tooling is detected but the parse yields nothing — a detection failure must never read as a green.

nuances.title: No artifact means no score, not a bad score
nuances.detail: On a stack measured from a committed artifact, the absence of an OpenAPI document or GraphQL SDL produces no report and the criterion stays unscored. That is the honest answer: we did not find the contract, which is not the same as finding an undocumented one.

nuances.title: N/A where there is no machine API
nuances.detail: A system with no machine-readable API surface — a batch service with no HTTP contract, for instance — is N/A and excluded, rather than scored zero for having nothing to describe. Ruby systems are declared N/A today; that is a decision carried from the pilot, not a finding about Ruby codebases.

nuances.title: What the REST parse does not expand
nuances.detail: Shared parameter macros (CommonParameters.* and similar) and compile-time parameter groups are not expanded, so parameters they inject are not counted, and only the `parameters do` / `properties do` block forms are parsed. Both limitations are published with the score rather than left for a reader to discover, because each makes the denominator smaller than the real surface.

criteria.name: Observable State
criteria.one_liner: The three pillars of observability — logs, traces, errors — are active in code, not merely installed.
criteria.what: Whether the system is instrumented to be observable — the three backend pillars (structured logging, distributed tracing, error/exception tracking) plus frontend error tracking — measured as active, not merely present. Each pillar is assessed on a declared → configured → exercised ladder.
criteria.why: If an agent (or anyone) breaks something, observability is how the failure is noticed. A pillar declared in the manifest but never wired up gives false confidence: the library is there and nothing is emitted. Systems an autonomous agent can safely change are the ones where breakage surfaces loudly.

how.tools: Headless static scan — dependency manifests (mix.exs / Gemfile / package.json), config files and source call-sites. No compile, no external scanner; the signal lists are in observability-signals.js in this repository.
how.anchors: The three pillars of observability (logs, traces, errors), and the "active, not just present" discipline — declared → configured → exercised.
how.scoring: Each pillar takes the highest rung it reaches: none 0.0, declared 2.0, configured 3.5, exercised 5.0. The criterion is the mean of the applicable pillars, equal weight. No hard-cap — under-instrumentation is an operability risk, not a security emergency.

nuances.title: Frontend pillar is N/A when there is no frontend
nuances.detail: The frontend error-tracking pillar is excluded from the mean (marked N/A and noted in coverage) when the system has no real frontend surface. Detected rather than hardcoded: a frontend manifest declaring a UI framework (vue/react/nuxt), or a non-trivial .vue/.tsx count. Expected N/A for backend-only services, whose criterion is then the mean of the three backend pillars.

nuances.title: Highest rung wins
nuances.detail: A pillar is scored at the strongest evidence found. Where code exercises the tool — real Logger., tracer or capture_exception call sites — the pillar is active whether or not the configuration heuristic matched. The config patterns are approximate; usage evidence is decisive.

nuances.title: LLM tracing is labelled, not counted as infra tracing
nuances.detail: Where every tracer a system declares traces the app or LLM pipeline rather than cross-service requests (langfuse, langsmith, openinference, @vercel/otel), the tracing finding says so. The pillar still scores on the ladder; the label stops a green being read as APM-grade distributed tracing, which is a different capability.

nuances.title: Stack caveats
nuances.detail: Elixir's Logger is in the standard library, so "structured logging exercised" leans on the structured-backend config signal rather than on raw Logger. calls. For Sentry-Vue, Sentry.init() effectively is the integration, so configured and exercised sit close together on the frontend pillar. AppSignal on Ruby auto-instruments Rails from config/appsignal.yml with few explicit calls, so it is detected through that YAML and namespace usage rather than by assuming explicit capture sites. Frontend error tracking requires a real reporting library or an explicit capture call (Sentry.captureException, Bugsnag.notify) — a bare Vue errorHandler is error handling, not tracking.

nuances.title: Runtime signals are out of scope
nuances.detail: Coverage percentages, alert effectiveness, staleness by traffic and a frontend RUM pillar are all runtime measurements. This criterion scores the static readiness kernel — what the repository shows — and nothing that requires a running system.

criteria.name: Test Coverage
criteria.one_liner: A test-discipline floor — enough automated coverage to change code safely.
criteria.what: Static test-coverage readiness: whether source files have tests, and whether CI enforces a coverage bar. A discipline floor, not a quality guarantee — coverage is not correctness.
criteria.why: Without a safety net of tests, neither an agent nor an engineer can refactor or ship with confidence.

how.tools: Static test↔source mapping, and coverage enforcement read from GitHub Actions workflows (minimum_coverage gates). The coverage library itself is a secondary audit label. No suite is run.
how.anchors: Two facets, mean of 2. Breadth: the fraction of source files with a paired test file, pooled across stacks. Discipline: coverage enforced in CI, graded on Google's 60/75/90 tiers, mean of the applicable stacks.
how.scoring: Breadth is linear — 5 × the fraction of source files with a paired test. Discipline is a rung per stack: none 0, tool configured but no threshold 2.0, enforced at a threshold graded on the Google tiers (60 → 3.5, 75 → 4.25, 90 → 5.0). The criterion is the mean of the two facets. No hard-cap.

nuances.title: Breadth is file presence, not line coverage
nuances.detail: A source file counts as tested when a test file pairs with it. Actual line coverage needs a compile, a database and secrets, none of which this scan has. The proxy reads generously and the report says so wherever it is quoted.

nuances.title: The pairing ignores paths, so it flatters
nuances.detail: Breadth pairs a source file to a test by basename stem, ignoring directory, so one user_test.exs marks every */user.ex as tested. A precise per-unit map needs the Clear Domain Boundaries code graph and comes with it.

nuances.title: minimum_coverage: 0 counts as configured, not enforced
nuances.detail: A coverage tool configured with a threshold of zero, or with none at all, earns the configured rung and not the enforced tier. A gate that passes with no tests is not a floor.

nuances.title: CI-gate detection reads GitHub Actions only
nuances.detail: Tool-config signals (coveralls.json, SimpleCov, vitest and jest thresholds) are CI-agnostic, but the gate signal is read from GitHub Actions workflow files. Every organisation on the benchmark today is on GitHub; GitLab, Jenkins, CircleCI and Azure are added when the first tenant that needs one arrives, rather than written blind.

nuances.title: Critical-path coverage is not measured
nuances.detail: Which paths matter most — the intersection of the code graph, churn, complexity and traffic — is not part of this criterion. Until it is, a high breadth number says tests exist, not that the right things are tested.

criteria.name: Deployment Safety
criteria.one_liner: Changes can be deployed safely and bad deploys recovered — progressive delivery, automated rollback, a gated staged pipeline, and independent deployability, as declared in the repo.
criteria.what: Four deployment-safety capabilities, detected from in-repo configuration (CI on any platform, IaC, Dockerfiles): progressive delivery (canary, blue-green), automated health-triggered rollback, pipeline safety (a staged staging→prod progression with CI gating), and independent deployability (each unit releasable on its own).
criteria.why: An agent or engineer that ships a change needs the deploy path to catch and recover from a bad release. Systems without progressive delivery or automated rollback fail loudly in production, and tightly-coupled deployables mean one change redeploys everything, widening the blast radius.

how.tools: Headless static scan of in-repo CI/CD config (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI), IaC and manifests (Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, Argo, Terraform, CodeDeploy), and Dockerfiles. Ecosystem-agnostic — no in-house CD system knowledge; no compile, no external scanner.
how.anchors: DORA deployment capabilities: progressive delivery, automated (health-triggered) rollback, deployment automation with CI gating, and a loosely-coupled, independently-deployable architecture.
how.scoring: Each of the three tool capabilities takes a none/basic/mature rung (0.0 / 3.5 / 5.0); independent deployability is binary (independent 5.0, coupled 2.0). The criterion is the mean of the four. No hard-cap.

nuances.title: Repo-visible only — readiness, not outcomes
nuances.detail: This measures deployment safety declared in the repository, not verified production behaviour. Automated rollback in particular often lives inside an external CD platform and is invisible to a clone scan, so such a system scores low on rollback even where its real deploys recover safely. That is deliberate: an agent working in the repository cannot see externalised safety either. Deployment frequency, lead time, change-failure rate and MTTR are runtime measurements and are not part of this criterion.

nuances.title: Ecosystem-agnostic signals
nuances.detail: Detection uses portable markers — Spinnaker, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, CodeDeploy, Helm --atomic, Kubernetes probes and progressDeadlineSeconds, Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK, merge_group, staging→prod workflows — and never in-house CD system names, so the criterion travels to any organisation.

nuances.title: The signal lists are approximate
nuances.detail: The marker lists and the independent-deployability heuristic (deployable units against deploy paths) are approximations tuned against real repositories before publishing, in the same way the Observable State and Codebase Simplicity signal lists were.

criteria.name: Codebase Simplicity
criteria.one_liner: Low cyclomatic complexity and low duplication, so canonical patterns are unambiguous for an agent.
criteria.what: Consolidation debt — over-complex functions and duplicated logic from rewrites and app merges that make it hard to tell which pattern is canonical. Two sub-metrics, averaged: cyclomatic complexity and code duplication.
criteria.why: Agents cannot operate safely where canonical patterns are ambiguous. Simpler code is more agentic-compatible — the thesis of the whole benchmark.

how.tools: Complexity: credo, rubocop and lizard are co-resident adapters selected per file extension — credo for .ex/.exs (standalone runner, no target compile), rubocop for .rb (Metrics/CyclomaticComplexity only), lizard for .js/.mjs/.cjs/.jsx/.ts/.tsx/.py and for the <script> block of .vue single-file components. Every material language in a repo is measured, so a polyglot repo is scored by several tools at once and the findings name each. Duplication on all stacks: jscpd. None of them compiles the target. Note that only lizard is version-pinned: rubocop, credo and jscpd resolve at run time, so two scans of the same code on different days can differ slightly.
how.anchors: McCabe cyclomatic complexity ≤ 10 (every adapter pinned to 10) · code duplication < 5% (jscpd's own default).
how.scoring: Complexity is the mean of a measured violation density and a CI enforcement rung. Density: 0 functions over CC 10 is green 5.0; above 0 it is graded per 1,000 lines of source. Enforcement: none 0, configured 2.0, enforced above the anchor 3.5, enforced at or below the anchor 5.0 — resolved per language, then pooled weighted by each language's share of the measured lines. Duplication: under 1% green, 1-5% amber (graded), over 5% red (graded). The criterion is the mean of complexity and duplication. Unlike Security, it has no hard-cap.

nuances.title: The aggregation is our convention, not a published anchor
nuances.detail: McCabe ≤ 10 per function is the published standard (McCabe 1976); turning a violation count into a score out of five is a choice this benchmark made. Density per 1,000 lines is used because it is size-normalised — a small codebase with one complex function and a large one with fifty tell different stories at the same raw count — and the raw counts are on the scorecard so the band need not be trusted in isolation. The 500-line materiality floor, below which a language is skipped rather than measured, is ours too. So is the enforcement ladder: the 3.5 rung for a gate enforced above 10 is a judgement call, not a standard, and it exists because we override ESLint's default of 20 down to 10 in our own measurement — accepting a repo's 20 as full marks would contradict the standard we hold ourselves to.

nuances.title: A gated repo's clean count describes the gate
nuances.detail: Where a repo enforces a complexity limit in CI, no function above it can merge, so a zero violation count is a property of the gate rather than an observation about the code. This is why enforcement is scored alongside the measured density: a clean count on an enforcing repo is evidence of sustained discipline, and a clean count on an ungated repo is evidence only about today's snapshot.

nuances.title: The enforcement rung is weighted by how much code it covers
nuances.detail: A gate protects in proportion to the amount of code it stands in front of, so each language's rung is weighted by that language's share of the measured lines rather than averaged flat. One umbrella enforces credo at 9 over 197k of its 298k measured lines and gates nothing else: an unweighted mean of [5.0, 0, 0, 0] reads 1.3, which describes a repo with essentially no complexity discipline, and that is not this one. Weighted, it reads 3.3. The more important half runs the other way — unweighted averaging flatters a repo that gates only a twentieth of its code, because one tiny gated language would count for as much as the large ungated one beside it.

nuances.title: Enforcement detection reads GitHub Actions only
nuances.detail: The CI gate is read from GitHub Actions workflow files. Every organisation on the benchmark today is on GitHub; other platforms are added when a tenant needs one, on the same basis as Test Coverage.

nuances.title: Complexity covers every material language in the repo
nuances.detail: Complexity is measured for every language above the 500-line floor, not for a single primary stack — an Elixir or Ruby system's frontend is measured alongside its backend. Violations and lines are both pooled before the density is computed, so a polyglot repo is not penalised for being polyglot. The per-language breakdown — which tool measured which language, over how many lines, finding how many violations — is in the audit block, because the headline count is a sum across several tools.

nuances.title: Residual gaps are reported, not silently dropped
nuances.detail: lizard cannot parse .vue directly, so each single-file component's <script> block is extracted and analysed with line numbers mapped back to the .vue file. Vue template logic — branching expressed in directives — stays unmeasured; no tool we have reads it. PL/pgSQL has no complexity tool and is reported by extension with its line count. Failed extractions, files skipped as generated or binary, and languages below the materiality floor are all counted in the scan report rather than disappearing.

nuances.title: Duplication measures code, not data
nuances.detail: jscpd runs with translations, locale and data files and docs excluded (*.po, *.json, *.csv, *.svg, *.md, locales/). Without that, data files dominate — one repo reads 14.99% raw and 5.89% code-only. The exclusion makes the percentage a simplicity signal rather than a count of how many translation strings repeat.

nuances.title: Elixir duplication runs through the Ruby tokenizer
nuances.detail: jscpd has no native Elixir tokenizer, so .ex/.exs are mapped to the Ruby one, which handles do/end block structure well enough for copy-paste detection. This is approximate and flagged as such; a native tokenizer would be more precise.

nuances.title: Complexity via a standalone Credo runner
nuances.detail: Credo runs from a throwaway project whose only dependency is Credo, pointed at the clone through files.included — so the target is never compiled and its private Hex and git dependencies are never fetched, the same headless sidestep Security uses. Credo's default file scope silently skips external paths, so the absolute clone path has to be set explicitly.

nuances.title: The violation count and the line count exclude the same files
nuances.detail: Vendored, generated and test code is excluded from both the violation count and the line denominator, from one shared definition rather than a per-tool list. This was wrong once and the findings were the evidence: 22 of one repo's 57 published violations came from vendored jQuery plugins and a Playwright test file, and both of another repo's came from a minified calendar bundle — files whose lines the denominator had already discarded. The reports were telling those teams to refactor code they did not write.

nuances.title: Allowances: findings judged acceptable
nuances.detail: A watchtower can record a finding it has already judged acceptable and give the reason. An allowance removes that finding from the score and keeps it in the report, marked, with the reason and who allowed it. Allowances do not apply to duplication, whose percentage comes from the tool's own totals rather than from a list of blocks, nor to criteria that measure an absence — allowing "no rollback configured" would be accepting a risk, not correcting a false positive. The mechanics are described under Security Posture.

criteria.name: Security Posture
criteria.one_liner: No exposed secrets, no known-vulnerable production dependencies, no high-severity code-security findings.
criteria.what: Three sub-metrics: secrets committed to the repo, dependency CVEs, and static application security findings. Together they answer whether the current tree is already clean enough to hand to something that ships code.
criteria.why: A system already leaking secrets or shipping vulnerable dependencies is not safe to hand to an autonomous agent. Security is the one dimension with a hard cap. The composite is a system's criterion scores averaged and rescaled to 100 (Red 0-40, Amber 41-70, Green 71-100); a critical finding here multiplies that number by 0.4, so the best a capped system can score is exactly 40 and it is still Red. The cap is inside the number rather than painted over it, which is why a score and its colour can never disagree — and scaling rather than clamping keeps capped systems ranked against each other, so it stays visible which one is closest to being fixable.

how.tools: gitleaks (secrets), trivy fs --scanners vuln (dependency CVEs over Hex, RubyGems and npm lockfiles), semgrep --config auto (SAST, all languages including Elixir, Ruby, JavaScript and Vue). All three are version-pinned; none compiles the target.
how.anchors: 0 confirmed exposed secrets · 0 Critical/High CVEs in direct production dependencies (CIS v8) · 0 high-severity SAST findings (OWASP Top 10 / CWE).
how.scoring: Each sub-metric scores 0-5 against its anchor and the criterion is their mean. Hard cap: any confirmed exposed secret, any critical production-dependency CVE, or any critical SAST finding forces the system's badge to Red.

nuances.title: Shared path triage (gitleaks and semgrep)
nuances.detail: Raw scanner output is overwhelmingly noise: secrets in test fixtures, mocks, seed data and VCR cassettes. A shared path allowlist (test/, spec/, __mocks__/, fixtures/, priv/data/seed/, cassette_library/, config/test.exs) is excluded from both scanners before scoring — the same fixture noise trips both. priv/static is deliberately not excluded: real committed keys live there. Raw and triaged counts are both kept for the audit trail.

nuances.title: Secrets: confirmed against review
nuances.detail: gitleaks' generic-api-key rule is low-precision — in config files it matches public identifiers (client ids, analytics tags, UUIDs, reCAPTCHA site keys) about as often as real credentials. Those hits go to a review bucket that is surfaced but does not hard-cap. High-precision rules — private keys, provider tokens — are confirmed and drive the cap. Real secrets still force Red; noisy generic matches are put in front of a human instead of sinking the badge.

nuances.title: Trivy scores direct dependencies only
nuances.detail: CVEs are attributed to their package's role, parsed from the manifests (mix.exs :only groups, package.json dependencies against devDependencies). Direct production dependencies score at full weight and can cap. Direct dev-only dependencies are discounted to medium and never cap — a dev-tool vulnerability is real but not production-reachable. Transitive dependencies are shown for information and not scored: they are unactionable without their direct parent, and scoring them made every system red on noise.

nuances.title: Semgrep hardening rules are remapped
nuances.detail: Some semgrep rules flag CI and workflow hardening recommendations rather than code vulnerabilities — non-SHA-pinned actions, secrets-inherit. These dominate raw high counts, so they are remapped to informational. Matching is by rule-id leaf, because --config auto emits ids shaped like <path>.<leaf>.<leaf>.

nuances.title: Audit trail
nuances.detail: Every result carries a raw → triaged → allowed record per scanner: the raw count, the triaged count, what was excluded and why, and how many findings were allowed. Any score can be followed back to the finding it came from.

nuances.title: Allowances: findings judged acceptable
nuances.detail: A watchtower can record a finding it has already judged acceptable — a public site key that reads as a secret, a CVE in a package only ever loaded in development. An allowance removes that finding from the score and keeps it in the report, marked, with the reason and who allowed it. It matches on the finding's own fields: a secret on file, rule and optionally line; a dependency CVE on package, advisory id, severity, installed version, manifest or prod/dev bucket. A line is the only way to tell two hits of the same rule in one file apart, and it is also what goes stale — code moves, and the entry then matches nothing, or matches whichever finding moved into its place. Every run reports how many findings each allowance absorbed and names those that absorbed none; that report, not the score, is what tells you the list is still doing its job. The list lives with the organisation that made the judgements rather than in the shared engine, and a malformed entry fails the whole file rather than being skipped, so no judgement is dropped quietly.
